title: It’s Good to Talk
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison joins the recent online argument about oracy by describing one Year 7 history lesson in which paired talk worked especially well. After a short teacher input on motte and bailey castles, students were assigned opposite sides of a question, given twenty seconds of silent thinking, and then two minutes of paired talk. The teacher finished by asking four students to report what their partner had said. Allison breaks the sequence into seven design features, among them talk coming after knowledge, a defined intellectual job for each student, silence before speech, an information gap, a time limit, and accountable listening. He links the routine to Durrington's Teaching PiPs and its emphasis on participation ratio. His conclusion is that purposeful talk does not happen by accident: it comes from the architecture around it, and the routine is simple enough to be habitual across subjects.
points: Talk comes after knowledge: students had just received teacher input, so the conversation was about history rather than generic opinion.
Assigning each partner a different side, advantages or disadvantages, gives both a defined job and creates a real reason to listen.
Twenty seconds of silent thinking before talk protects slower processors and stops the quickest thinker setting the conversation.
Asking students to report their partner's idea rather than their own makes listening accountable and gives the later whole-class sharing something to build on.
The routine needs no special resources, so its value lies in the sequencing of thinking, speaking, and listening, which makes it easy to transfer across subjects.
quotes: The teacher deliberately engineered a sequence in which students first acquire something worth thinking about, think independently, rehearse and articulate their thinking, and then listen carefully enough to represent somebody else’s thinking.
Good classroom talk depends on students having something substantive to talk about. It makes the subsequent conversation historical rather than generic.
Both students know exactly what they are responsible for contributing. There is much less opportunity for one confident student to do all the intellectual work.

That gives students time to retrieve the relevant knowledge, formulate an idea and prepare what they might say. It particularly supports students who need a little more processing time, rather than allowing the quickest thinker to determine the conversation.
The teacher doesn’t ask students to report their own idea. This makes listening matter.

The learning from this is that purposeful talk needs to be designed. In this example, the teacher has deliberately controlled what students know, what they think about, who thinks about what, when they speak, what they listen for and what they subsequently do with the conversation.

The sophistication lies not in the activity itself, but in the careful sequencing of thinking, speaking and listening. It is a great example of how a few small teaching decisions can turn “talk to your partner” into genuinely purposeful classroom talk.
